Orchot Tzadikim 9:59: And if he does this, he may trust in the Blessed Creator that He will deal kindly with him just as He dealt kindly with all the prophets and the pious. Whoever trusts in the Lord possesses a very great trait, and a person needs great self-improvement before he arrives at the depth of trust.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:60: Whoever trusts in the Lord is prepared to receive kindness, as it is written (Psalms 32:10), "but he who trusts in the Lord, kindness shall surround him." And it does not merely say "shall reach him" but "shall surround him," because the one who trusts must breach several gaps that are not good for him in this world: he must rebuke the multitude, even though he must fear them, lest they harm him in body or in property. He must also give up hope of his relatives and friends, so as not to join with them when they do not walk a good path, and so as not to flatter them. He must also abandon many worldly affairs, and free his heart from the vanities of the world to occupy himself with Torah. This requires great trust, and therefore the verse says: "kindness shall surround him."
Orchot Tzadikim 9:61: And trust is impossible without faith, as it is written (Psalms 9:11), "and those who know Your Name shall trust in You." For those who know His great Name and recognize His greatness and His might, and who believe with a whole heart — these are able to trust in Him. For trust and faith are partners: without faith there is no trust. And faith is the head of the Torah, as it is written (Exodus 20), "I am the Lord your God... you shall have no other gods before Me." And if one does not believe, what good does his Torah do him? And when a person believes from the depth of his heart that the Creator will fulfill everything written in the Torah — bringing calamities upon the sinner, and paying reward to those who fulfill it — then he keeps the Torah. For no thief or robber, if he knew for certain that he would be put to death for his theft and robbery and could not escape, would fail to refrain; but all thieves and robbers always trust that they will be saved, and therefore do whatever their heart desires. So too the sinner: had he truly believed in the greatness of his punishment, he would not sin.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:62: Therefore the entire Torah is contained within faith, as it is written (Habakkuk 2:4), "but the righteous shall live by his faith." And of Abraham it is said (Genesis 15:6), "and he believed in the Lord, and He counted it to him as righteousness" — and this was not written of any of his other good deeds.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:63: And of Moses it is written (Numbers 12:7), "he is faithful in all My house." And we say in the Midrash (Shemot Rabbah 22:23): great is faith before the Holy One, blessed be He, for by the merit of the faith our fathers believed, the Holy Spirit rested upon them and they said the [Song at the Sea], as it is said (Exodus 14:31-15:1), "and they believed in the Lord and in Moses His servant; then Moses and the children of Israel sang."
Orchot Tzadikim 9:64: And they were redeemed by the merit of the faith they believed, as it is written (ibid. 4:31), "and the people believed." And they said there: whoever accepts even one commandment with faith is worthy of having the Holy Spirit rest upon him. And the exiles will be gathered in by the merit of faith, as it is said (Song of Songs 4:8), "look from the top of Amanah [faithfulness]"; and it says (Hosea 2:22), "and I will betroth you to Me in faithfulness."
Orchot Tzadikim 9:65: And now let us return to the matter of joy: whoever believes with a whole heart and trusts in the help of the Rock is joyful forever. And he bears everything, like a sick person who swallows bitter medicines for the sake of healing. And whoever bears things patiently is free from worldly worry. Also, one who bears things patiently is content with the little he has, for he says: it is enough for me, whatever the Creator has decreed for me.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:66: And now consider and see that joy encompasses everything: for every person who worries about this world has no rest, and constantly schemes to earn money, and is never content with what God has allotted him. Therefore whoever rejoices in his own portion is rich even if he is poor (Avot 4:1), for he rejoices in God, who is his portion and his inheritance. And so it is written (Psalms 119:57), "I have said, O Lord, that my portion is to observe Your words"; and it says (ibid. 105:3), "let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice."
Orchot Tzadikim 9:67: And this trait is found in the souls of the righteous, who are in complete pleasantness in their service, and in great joy in their asceticism, as it is said (ibid. 32:11), "be glad in the Lord and rejoice, you righteous, and shout for joy, all you upright in heart." And it says (ibid. 97:11), "light is sown for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart."
Orchot Tzadikim 9:68: Therefore let every person place his joy on the Torah, and at the time he performs the commandments, let him rejoice in his heart that he has merited to be a servant of the supreme King, whom the beings on high bow down to. And so David said (ibid. 119:162), "I rejoice at Your word, like one who finds great spoil." And whoever performs the commandments with joy has a thousand times the reward of one for whom the commandments are a burden. Abraham and David were occupied with Torah the entire day, glorifying and praising the Holy One, blessed be He, with songs and praises, raising their voices in joy.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:69: And then he succeeds in all his ways and his understanding is good, and He sends the Holy Spirit within him, and his heart is joyful and filled with love of the Holy One, blessed be He, and his soul is bound in gladness, and secrets and novel insights from above are revealed to him, because he feared the Blessed Lord and was upright, and this understanding entered within him. And this is what Solomon said (Song of Songs 5:6), "my soul went out when he spoke"; "and my innermost being will rejoice when your lips speak what is right" (Proverbs 23:16). And so David said (Psalms 103:1), "bless, O my soul [the Lord]" — because the soul comes from an exalted source and rises upward, and when it knows the matter of its own secret, it will love its Creator and treasure His commandments. And when the soul reaches the level and rank to which it is akin, it will then unite Him within its innermost places and delight in its inner chambers, and at every time and every moment will yearn for love of Him, and remember Him at night upon its bed — then the Blessed Lord sends into it the desire for joy, and the heart will burn and be kindled from the abundance of the desire of love, as the matter is said (Isaiah 61:10), "I will greatly rejoice in the Lord, my soul shall be joyful in my God." Happy is the soul that merits that joy.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:70: And the Divine Presence rests only through joy (Shabbat 30b). And none of the prophets prophesied whenever they wished, but rather they would compose their minds and sit joyful and glad-hearted, and then prophesy; for prophecy does not rest through laziness, nor through sadness, but through joy. Therefore the disciples of the prophets would bring before them a lute, a drum, and a harp, and seek prophecy, as it is written (2 Kings 3:15), "and it came to pass, when the minstrel played, that the hand of the Lord came upon him."
Orchot Tzadikim 9:71: The glory of the soul is this: that it glory in the splendor of the joy with which it rejoices in the Lord, and that the radiance of its awe shine forth to display the preciousness of its glory, and that the light of its yearning be sweet to its Maker in the love and longing and desire for the exalted craving, to crown itself with the crown of the beauty of pure and clean thoughts, and it will moan from the greatness of its rejoicing for its Beloved, the exalted Beloved, and bind itself in bonds of affection, and seek out and search after the virtues to become illumined by the light of life. And at the time it is uplifted and grows and rolls onward to know the holiness of its Maker, and cleaves in faith to the Blessed Creator, then it spreads itself in a renewal of joy and expands in its gladness. At that hour it is sanctified with the sanctity of the Holy of Holies, and then it longs for and finds favor before the King of kings, and at that time it becomes precious and beautiful and adorned in the splendor of the pride and strength of its own glory. And then the One above will treasure it, to make its splendor shine forth, to bring it into chambers of radiance and to bind it in the bond of life. And may the Merciful One place us among the people of His service who rejoice.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:72: There is a further benefit in joy, as with the two men of whom it was said that they were among the people of the World to Come because they were joyful men, and when they saw a sad man, they would cheer him up; and when they saw two people quarreling with one another, they would tell them words of jest until they made peace between them. And likewise regarding halachic study: one begins with words of jest to open the heart to study with joy — but not the joy of vulgarity and the joy of vanities, but rather words of the commandments that gladden the heart, as it is written (Psalms 19:9), "the precepts of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart" — and all this is with the joy of a commandment.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:73: And likewise when a person has some suffering, he should rejoice as well. And so our Sages said (Bava Metzia 85a): sufferings are precious. And our Sages further said (Ta'anit 8a): whoever rejoices in the sufferings that come upon him brings salvation to the world. And he should accustom his mouth to say, "this too is for the good" (ibid. 21a), or "whatever the Merciful One does, He does for the good" (Berachot 60b), for there are several bad things whose end is good, and so our Sages expounded on this verse (Isaiah 12:1), "I will thank You, O Lord, for though You were angry with me, Your anger has turned away and You comfort me": a parable of two men who went to cross by ship. One of them had a thorn stuck in his foot, so that he was unable to board the ship, and his fellow boarded the ship to cross. This one began cursing his day. Some days later he heard that the ship had sunk and the men aboard it had died. Then this one began praising the Blessed Creator, for he saw that this had happened in order to keep him alive (Niddah 31a). Therefore let a person rejoice in sufferings and other harms that come upon him, for he does not know what good is destined to come to him from them. And so did Nachum Ish Gamzu ("this too") (Ta'anit 21a).
Orchot Tzadikim 9:74: It is also good to make a bridegroom and bride rejoice, as it is said (Jeremiah 7:34), "the voice of gladness and the voice of joy, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride." And one must be very careful not to make them rejoice with vulgar speech, for such joy is [really] wrath and anger and fury; nor should there be joy of men and women mingled together, for such joy is levity. And even at a time of eulogy and mourning we say (Sukkah 52a): men separately and women separately — how much more so at a time of joy. And we expound: "and walk humbly with your God" (Micah 6:8) — this refers to accompanying the dead and bringing a bride to the wedding canopy (Sukkah 49b).
Orchot Tzadikim 9:75: One should also rejoice on Sabbaths and festivals and Purim, for all of these are in remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt and in remembrance of the wonders He performed for His chosen ones. Therefore let him rejoice in his heart when he remembers the kindnesses of the Omnipresent, and the greatness of His good deeds toward those who do His will. And for this reason people prepare delicacies and precious garments, and drink wine to gladden the heart. But one must be careful not to rejoice in that joy over vanities; rather, he should place his joy upon love of the Blessed Lord, and yearn in the delight of love of the Rock, and rejoice and be glad in the joy of the Lord of all, who commanded that one indulge and rejoice on that day. Also, in those days he should remember the pleasantness of the World to Come, which is the ultimate pleasantness. And it is fitting for a person, at the time he indulges in pleasures, to remember the great [future] pleasures and long for them, as it is written (Isaiah 58:14), "then you shall delight yourself in the Lord."
Orchot Tzadikim 9:76: He should also rejoice when he sees the joy of the wicked and the pleasures of transgressors, and think: if this is given to those who transgress His will, how much more so to those who do His will (Nedarim 50b). And of this David said (Psalms 4:8), "You have put gladness in my heart, more than in the time their grain and wine increased." This is like a parable of a king who invited guests, and when they arrived at the king's courtyard they saw that the dogs were eating geese and chickens; then the guests rejoiced and said: if the dogs fare so well, how much more shall we, who are invited to dine with the king (Midrash Tehillim 4:11)?!
Orchot Tzadikim 9:77: And it is forbidden to rejoice over the good of the vanities of this world. For whoever recognizes this world will not rejoice in its good, and will not rejoice in any matter except one that brings him to the service of the Blessed Omnipresent.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:78: A person must not rejoice over something good for himself that comes with a mishap for others. For instance, a person who has produce should not rejoice if there is high cost and famine, for he should not rejoice at the world's calamity for the sake of his own benefit. Nor should he rejoice at a person's death, even though he stands to inherit from him or gain other benefits. In sum: he should not rejoice at anyone's misfortune for his own enjoyment, and of this it is said (Leviticus 19:18), "and you shall love your fellow as yourself." And he should accustom his heart to be joyful when others have good things. And he should rejoice all the more upon seeing people pursuing the commandments to do the will of the Blessed Creator.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:79: And he should not rejoice or fill his mouth with laughter, for now all joy has grown bitter (Berachot 31a); for on the day our holy Rabbi [Yehuda HaNasi] would laugh, calamity would come upon the world (Nedarim 50b). And likewise, up to this point, Rabbi Yirmiyah tried to bring Rabbi Zeira to laughter, but he did not laugh (Niddah 23a).
Orchot Tzadikim 9:80: And when is there cause to rejoice and laugh? At the time the Divine Presence returns to Zion, which is a great joy, as it is written (Psalms 126:2), "then our mouth shall be filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing; then it shall be said among the nations, the Lord has done great things for these" (Berachot 31a).
Orchot Tzadikim 10:2: Worry. This trait is bad in most of its effects, and it is recognizable on the entire face, as it is written (Genesis 40:6), "and he saw them, and behold, they were sad"; and it is written (Nehemiah 2:2), "why is your face sad, seeing you are not sick?"
Orchot Tzadikim 10:3: And one of the sages said: I find no sign of worry at all among people of exalted souls. Whoever worries about attaining anything in this world is very disgraceful, and this trait is not found at all in people who trust in the Lord and believe in Him.
Orchot Tzadikim 10:4: Worry and sorrow consume the heart, and are an illness of the body. And the worst worry of all worries is one that leads a person to pursue transgressions, for when he cannot find whatever his heart desires, he worries and grieves. Whoever worries about this world is very far from Torah, commandments, and prayer. Therefore let him take great care to correct this trait, to remove it from himself. And there is no need to elaborate on its evil, for all the good things that come from joy are the opposite of worry.
Orchot Tzadikim 10:5: And now consider! There are also good paths within worry, as the prophet said (Lamentations 3:39), "why should a living man complain, a man for his sins?" The sinner must magnify sorrow in his heart and sigh in bitterness of heart, for having rebelled against the Maker of all.
Orchot Tzadikim 10:6: If he loses a single coin, it is hard in a person's eyes; and if he loses his wealth and comes out stripped of his possessions, does his soul not mourn over it? And likewise over troubles, his pain and sorrow are constant in his heart. How much more fitting is it that he grieve and sigh over having rebelled against the Blessed Lord, and not remembered His kindnesses and His good deeds toward him.
Orchot Tzadikim 10:7: Know that the levels of teshuvah all depend on the essence of the sorrow. For sorrow comes from the purity of the soul, the supernal soul, and therefore sorrow and worry are accepted before the Blessed Lord. And the parable for this is: a king whom the members of his own household, who are close to him and who are among the honored nobles of the land, have angered — he shows them more grace and compassion than his compassion for the distant and the lowly. Therefore the Blessed Lord has compassion on the soul that is pained and worried over its sins. And so David said (Psalms 38:10), "Lord, all my desire is before You, and my sighing is not hidden from You."
Orchot Tzadikim 10:8: Tears come from sorrow and worry. And behold, the gates of tears were never locked (Bava Metzia 59a), as it is written (Psalms 119:136), "streams of water run down my eyes, because they do not keep Your Torah"; and it is written (ibid. 38:19), "for I will declare my iniquity, I will be sorrowful for my sin." And a person should always take sorrow into his heart over what has passed, and worry about the future, and always fear that he has not completed the requirement of teshuvah. And it is written (Proverbs 28:14), "happy is the man who is always fearful,"
Orchot Tzadikim 10:9: even if he is now completely innocent and righteous, let him always fear that sin might come into his hand. And so we find with Jacob: even though the Holy One, blessed be He, said to him, "and I will keep you wherever you go" (Genesis 28:15), he still feared lest sin cause harm. And so David said (Psalms 27:13), "had I not believed I would see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living [I would have despaired]" — even though he knew he was completely pious, he feared lest sin cause him to miss the pleasantness of the righteous (Berachot 4a).
Orchot Tzadikim 10:10: And he should always worry lest his service not be accepted before the Blessed Omnipresent, and lest he be among those of whom it is said (Isaiah 1:12), "who has required this of your hand, to trample My courts."
Orchot Tzadikim 10:11: Therefore let him gain more courage. There is a story of a certain sage who saw a man worrying. He said to him: if your worry is about this world, may the exalted Lord lessen your worry; but if your worry is about the World to Come, may the Blessed Lord increase your worry upon your worry.
Orchot Tzadikim 10:12: And worry is useful regarding Torah study, in that one constantly reviews it, lest he forget.
Orchot Tzadikim 10:13: Worry is also useful in that a person will not quarrel with anyone needlessly, for he fears lest harm come to him from the dispute.
Orchot Tzadikim 10:14: But at night, when a person rises to study, he should not fear demons upon rising from his bed, but should think: how many people walk alone at night and suffer no harm — and he should trust in the Blessed Lord, and rise without fear.
Orchot Tzadikim 10:15: A teacher and a pious man living far from his town should not refrain from going there to study out of fear of the roads, in the manner the lazy man said (Proverbs 22:13), "there is a lion outside, I shall be murdered in the streets!" Rather, he should think that most people travel and are not harmed; so too he should not refrain out of fear, for those on a mission to perform a commandment are not harmed (Pesachim 8b).
Orchot Tzadikim 10:16: In sum: in all his worries and sorrows he should direct his intent toward Heaven.
Orchot Tzadikim 10:17: If a relative of his dies, he should mourn, weep, and grieve, for perhaps the person died because of his own sin — for because of the fathers, children die — and behold, it is as though he himself killed him; and he should do teshuvah and make fences [against sin], and supplicate the Blessed Creator.
Orchot Tzadikim 10:18: If a worthy person dies, he should grieve and weep for him, and those tears the Holy One, blessed be He, counts and stores away in His treasury, as it is said (Psalms 56:9), "put my tears into Your bottle; are they not in Your book?"
